How might textual ecologies prepare for such an archive? Drawing on theories of dark archives, disaster librarianship, and “post-apocalyptic computing,” this chapter develops a speculative preservation framework that treats redundancy, community mirroring, and federated metadata as anticipatory responses to (textual) ecological instability. One way in which this has traditionally been effected is through the use of gothic tropes to render new technologies as frightful or vampiric upon either labour or life. In this chapter, I explore the ways that gothic aspects are applied to the new breed of large language models, broadly dubbed AI. Taking a base history of artificial life and its intersection with gothic literatures, such as Frankenstein, but also more contemporary touchstones, this chapter aims to understand how gothic rhetorics influence societal uptake and acceptance or rejection of new technological inventions. We tested whether such unchosen alternative action paths leave traces in memory. Across two behavioural exper-

iments, participants solved a modified Tower of London (ToL) task in which each problem afforded two alterna-

tive and equivalent optimal solution paths. They then undertook a recognition test in which they viewed configu-

rations of the ToL drawn either from the chosen path, the unchosen path, or from new, unviewed configurations.

Participants were consistently more likely to judge (falsely) that they had previously seen configurations from

the unchosen but plausible path, compared to novel configurations. Signal detection analyses further showed re-

duced discriminability and a more liberal decision criterion for alternative-path configurations compared to con-

trol novel configurations. Unchosen action alternatives may be difficult to distinguish from actions that are actu-

ally executed, but may have a feeling of familiarity that leads to an “old” response. This effect replicated when

novel items were matched to alternative items in visual similarity, ruling out explanations based on perceptual

confusability. The results are consistent with the idea that action planning generates representations of unchosen

alternatives that can persist and bias later memory, even if not executed. Planning therefore leaves behind more

than a route toward action goals: it also leaves mnemonic traces of paths not taken","tags":["PS"],"fulltextStatus":"disabled","subjects":["PS"],"oai":"oai:eprints.bbk.ac.uk.oai2:57865","deleted":"ALLOWED","disabled":false,"journals":[],"repositories":[],"repositoryDocument":{"id":757454717,"depositedDate":"","publishedDate":"","updatedDate":"","acceptedDate":"","createdDate":""},"urls":[{"url":"http://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106701","type":"fulltext"},{"url":"https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/57865/3/57865.pdf","type":"fulltext"}],"lastUpdate":"2026-09-14T07:38:39+01:00","setSpecs":[],"license":"","orcids":[],"sdg":[]},{"acceptedDate":"","authors":[{"name":"Eve, Martin Paul"}],"contributors":[],"createdDate":"2025-12-08T06:29:18+00:00","dataProvider":{"id":8,"name":"Birkbeck Institutional Research Online","url":"https://api.core.ac.uk/v3/data-providers/8","logo":"https://api.core.ac.uk/data-providers/8/logo"},"depositedDate":"2025-12-05T10:12:04+00:00","documentType":[],"versions":[],"doi":"","downloadUrl":"","fullText":"","id":684672624,"identifiers":{"doi":null,"oai":"oai:eprints.bbk.ac.uk.oai2:56615"},"title":"The Dark Web","language":null,"publishedDate":"2027-07-10T01:00:00+01:00","publisher":"The MIT Press","references":[],"sourceFulltextUrls":[],"updatedDate":null,"yearPublished":"2027","links":[{"type":"display","url":"https://core.ac.uk/outputs/684672624"}],"abstract":"With 5.52 billion internet users in 2024, the world wide web is today at least as prevalent as any of its predecessor media forms. In truth, the internet is everywhere and its terminologies – “to Google” – have entered the public lexicon. However, beneath the surface veneer of this twenty-first century convenience lurks another layer of the internet, normally hidden from view. This so-called “dark web”, a space of illicit markets and heavily encrypted communications that encourage anonymity, is powered by a series of sophisticated technologies.



This introductory book offers a concise sociological and technical analysis of the technologies that make up this dark web, charting the histories, technicalities, and uses for a range of different underground services. Assuming an interested, but not necessarily technical, reader, this book presents clear technological analyses and insightful sociological critiques of the technologies in question. Covering underground technologies and services such as The Onion Routing Project (Tor), hidden web services, Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), cryptocurrency and privacy coins such as Bitcoin (BTC) and Monero (XMR), and dark markets, the book also speaks to the legality and ethics, not only of these tools, but of the services to which they facilitate access.

Drawing on long-term, multi-sited ethnographic research and engaging with anthropological perspectives on ‘the shadow state’, this chapter specifically connects transnational adoption to the Guatemalan conflict (1960-1996) and argues that adoption flows from Guatemala to the Global North considerably intensified in the periods of harshest political repression, military counter-insurgency and genocidal violence. The chapter reviews the system of legal exceptionalism that enabled the transnational movement of children during the second part of the 20th century up until December 2007, when legal reforms suspended the flows of adoptees to the Global North. It then focuses on two paradigmatic cases that illustrate the nexus between transnational adoptions, forced disappearance, and genocide. First, I consider a case of forced disappearance that took place in 1983, at the height of counter-insurgency campaigns, when the Guatemalan Army abducted a group of children from a village of internally displaced Maya Poqomchi' and Maya Q'eqchi' communities in the region of Alta Verapaz. Following time spent in the custody of a religious order in Guatemala City, the children were gradually moved to Italy through informal transnational adoption networks and were adopted by Italian families. Second, I review a case of children who were abducted through deception during the 1980s. They were temporarily held in children’s homes managed by the Guatemalan state or by private individuals and were eventually adopted in Belgium, where a local organisation acted as intermediary. Whilst the first case illustrates how child abduction was deployed as a tool of genocidal counter-insurgency in the context of military assaults against Maya communities, the second case shows the progressive consolidation of transnational adoption circuits, the continued reliance on well-established practices of child abduction and forced removal, and the systematic forgery of documents up until 2006, when the Law of Adoptions came into force. The chapter concludes with a reflection on Guatemalan transnational adoptees’ activism and its significance for an understanding of the shadow circuits of adoption, genocide and the Guatemalan conflict","tags":["SS"],"fulltextStatus":"disabled","subjects":["SS"],"oai":"oai:eprints.bbk.ac.uk.oai2:51562","deleted":"ALLOWED","disabled":false,"journals":[],"repositories":[],"repositoryDocument":{"id":739600522,"depositedDate":"","publishedDate":"2027-01-01T00:00:00+00:00","updatedDate":"","acceptedDate":"","createdDate":""},"urls":[{"url":"https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/51562/1/51562.pdf","type":"fulltext"}],"lastUpdate":"2026-08-31T06:51:41+01:00","setSpecs":[],"license":"","orcids":[],"sdg":[]},{"acceptedDate":"","authors":[{"name":"Griffiths, Dilwyn"}],"contributors":[],"createdDate":"2026-08-24T06:21:13+01:00","dataProvider":{"id":8,"name":"Birkbeck Institutional Research Online","url":"https://api.core.ac.uk/v3/data-providers/8","logo":"https://api.core.ac.uk/data-providers/8/logo"},"depositedDate":"2026-08-17T14:28:48+01:00","documentType":[],"versions":[],"doi":"","downloadUrl":"","fullText":"","id":752783466,"identifiers":{"doi":null,"oai":"oai:eprints.bbk.ac.uk.oai2:57835"},"title":"Financial regulatory rulemaking in the European Union: when expertise meets politics","language":null,"publishedDate":"2027-02-10T00:00:00+00:00","publisher":"Palgrave Macmillan","references":[],"sourceFulltextUrls":[],"updatedDate":null,"yearPublished":"2027","links":[{"type":"display","url":"https://core.ac.uk/outputs/752783466"}],"abstract":"Book synopsis: This book provides the first comprehensive examination of the European Union’s binding technical standards regime, a specialized form of administrative rulemaking in EU financial services regulation. Drafted by the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs) rather than the Commission, these standards were originally conceived as a narrow and depoliticized instrument for addressing technical matters rather than policy issues. But they have instead evolved into a central component of the EU financial services rulebook, often dealing with politically salient and contested regulatory issues. This has led to recurring tensions between the ESAs and the EU institutional partners over the scope and content of individual standards.



Drawing on both rational choice and historical institutionalist perspectives, and combining detailed case studies and quantitative surveys, the book analyses all the stages of the technical standards process: from the negotiation of the framework legislation and decisions on delegated legislative empowerments, to the drafting, contestation on and adoption of the standards themselves. It provides a detailed examination of the institutions’ strategies and actions, using both formal and informal powers, and how the ESAs respond to their involvement in the standards-making process. In doing so, it also addresses wider questions about the relationship between politics and expertise in regulatory leakage?","language":null,"publishedDate":null,"publisher":"Elsevier","references":[],"sourceFulltextUrls":["http://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2026.128789","https://eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/57966/3/57966a.pdf"],"updatedDate":null,"yearPublished":"2027","links":[{"type":"display","url":"https://core.ac.uk/outputs/758485265"}],"abstract":"Amid the rapid reconfiguration of the global climate governance regime, border carbon adjustments (BCAs) have intensified the imbalance in the international allocation of mitigation responsibilities due to their extraterritorial and trade‐related nature. Carbon tariffs based on life-cycle carbon footprints are reshaping international

competitiveness while imposing additional mitigation burdens on developing economies. Using a multi-regional computable general equilibrium model based on the GTAP-E database, this study systematically evaluates the economic, environmental, and welfare impacts of alternative carbon pricing regimes, including

unilateral carbon tariffs, globally coordinated carbon pricing, and differentiated carbon taxes. The results reveal that carbon tariffs generate substantial responsibility-shifting effects, benefiting advanced economies while imposing disproportionate adjustment costs on developing countries. In contrast, globally coordinated carbon taxes and cost-equity–based differentiated carbon pricing achieve superior mitigation efficiency while preserving development equity, representing a more viable pathway toward a just low-carbon transition.
